Yes. 

The story makes remarkably sophisticated use of **metaphor**, both at the sentence level and as an overarching structural device. 

Throughout the narrative, the author uses vivid, original figurative language to establish mood and reveal character—such as describing the burned chair's backrest as a "blackened ribcage of wood," the couple standing "with the settled patience of trees," and the woman's grief as "some conflagration I couldn't see [that] had taken half of her and left the rest standing, leaning against things, waiting at curbs." 

Furthermore, the central elements of the story—the half-burned kitchen chair and the rising floodwaters—function as deeply resonant extended metaphors. The chair, "ruined in one part and untouched in another," serves as a physical manifestation of the couple's devastating loss (implied by the woman holding her grocery bag "the way women hold infants" and the vision of "three settings" at the table). The flood, which foreshadows the literal storm when the narrator compares his unemployed hours to a "floodplain," becomes a metaphor for the inescapable, invisible currents of grief that eventually return what was lost to the couple's doorstep.
